legend: Monocarp is the coach of the Berland State University programming teams. He decided to compose a problemset for a training session for his teams.

Monocarp has n%%ZSMJ0%% problems that none of his students have seen yet. The i%%ZSMJ1%%-th problem has a topic ai%%ZSMJ2%% (an integer from 1%%ZSMJ3%% to 200000%%ZSMJ4%%) and a difficulty bi%%ZSMJ5%% (an integer from 1%%ZSMJ6%% to 200000%%ZSMJ7%%). All problems are different, that is, there are no two problems that have the same topic and difficulty at the same time.
Monocarp decided to select exactly 3%%ZSMJ8%% problems from n%%ZSMJ9%% problems for the problemset. The problems should satisfy at least one of two conditions (possibly, both):
the topics of all three selected problems are different;
the difficulties of all three selected problems are different.
Your task is to determine the number of ways to select three problems for the problemset.
input: The first line contains an integer n%%ZSMJ10%% (3≤n≤200000%%ZSMJ11%%) — the number of problems that Monocarp has.
In the i%%ZSMJ12%%-th of the following n%%ZSMJ13%% lines, there are two integers ai%%ZSMJ14%% and bi%%ZSMJ15%% (1≤ai,bi≤200000%%ZSMJ16%%) — the topic and the difficulty of the i%%ZSMJ17%%-th problem.
It is guaranteed that there are no two problems that have the same topic and difficulty at the same time.
output: Print the number of ways to select three training problems that meet either of the requirements described in the statement.
note: In the first example, you can take the following sets of three problems:
Thus, the number of ways is equal to three.
